items.stem: In a 350–450 word narrative, what is usually the best approach to plot?
options: A single focused incident with one main turning point
A story covering a whole lifetime
items.answer: A single focused incident with one main turning point
items.markingKey: Short compositions reward focus and development over many events.

items.stem: This plan uses a linear structure: ‘Morning: the boy finds the dog. Afternoon: he hides it. Evening: his father discovers it.’ Explain how this structure could make the story more effective.
items.answer: Linear: events follow in time order.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for identifying linear; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: events follow in time order.

items.stem: This plan uses a dual timeline structure: ‘Alternate chapters between a girl in 1965 and her granddaughter today, revealing a family secret.’ Explain how this structure could make the story more effective.
items.answer: Dual timeline: two time periods run in parallel and illuminate each other.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for identifying dual timeline; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: two time periods run in parallel and illuminate each other.

items.stem: Identify the structure in this plan and explain one advantage and one risk of using it in an exam composition: ‘Begin with the funeral and move backwards, scene by scene, to the first meeting.’
items.answer: Reverse chronology: events are told backwards, so the reader knows the outcome and focuses on causes. Risk: confusing time shifts or running out of words before the resolution.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for reverse chronology; 1 for an advantage; 1 for a risk; further marks for developed explanation.

items.stem: Plan a narrative composition called ‘The Silence’ using a frame narrative structure. Outline the opening, the rising action, the climax and the resolution in one or two lines each.
items.answer: Model: opening that hooks (consistent with a frame narrative structure); rising complications; a single clear climax; a resolution that links back to the title ‘The Silence’.
items.markingKey: Award up to 5 marks from: structure clearly frame narrative; focused plot; clear climax; resolution earned and linked to the title; realistic for 350–450 words.

items.stem: Write a story with the title ‘The Key’. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach for ‘The Key’: plan a single focused conflict; hook in the first line; build to a clear climax; resolve with an image or line that links back to the title.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Indicative content: engaging opening; convincing characters and setting; deliberate structure with a clear turning point; controlled pace and tension; effective, earned ending; narrative voice sustained.

items.stem: Identify the structure in this plan and explain one advantage and one risk of using it in an exam composition: ‘Open at the bus stop in the rain; end at the same bus stop a year later.’
items.answer: Circular: returning to the opening setting shows how the character has changed. Risk: confusing time shifts or running out of words before the resolution.
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks from: 1 for circular; 1 for an advantage; 1 for a risk; further marks for developed explanation.

items.stem: What makes a narrative voice ‘distinctive’?
options: A consistent, recognisable personality conveyed through vocabulary, rhythm and attitude
Using as many characters as possible
items.answer: A consistent, recognisable personality conveyed through vocabulary, rhythm and attitude
items.markingKey: E.g. the dry humour of a teenage narrator.

items.stem: This extract uses a second-person narrator: ‘You wake before the alarm. You lie still, listening to the rain, and you remember what day it is.’ Explain the effect of this voice on the reader.
items.answer: Second-person narrator: ‘you’ places the reader inside the experience.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying second-person narrator; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: ‘you’ places the reader inside the experience.

items.stem: This extract uses a unreliable narrator: ‘I did not take the money. I merely borrowed it without asking, which is completely different.’ Explain the effect of this voice on the reader.
items.answer: Unreliable narrator: the narrator’s self-justification shows their account cannot be trusted.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for identifying unreliable narrator; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: the narrator’s self-justification shows their account cannot be trusted.

items.stem: Identify the narrative voice, explain how it is created, and rewrite the extract using a different voice: ‘bus late again rain in my shoes what did she mean by that look why do I always say the wrong thing’
items.answer: Stream of consciousness: unpunctuated, racing thoughts mimic the mind’s flow. The rewrite should change perspective, vocabulary and attitude consistently.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for stream of consciousness; 1 for how it is created; remaining mark(s) for a consistent rewrite in a new voice.

items.stem: Identify the narrative voice, explain how it is created, and rewrite the extract using a different voice: ‘The man next door is a spy. I know because he has three bins and nobody needs three bins.’
items.answer: Naive narrator: the child’s comic logic reveals innocence. The rewrite should change perspective, vocabulary and attitude consistently.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for naive narrator; 1 for how it is created; remaining mark(s) for a consistent rewrite in a new voice.

items.stem: Write a story in which the narrator is a person who has just moved to a new country. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: decide what a person who has just moved to a new country notices and misses; give them a characteristic way of speaking; let the reader infer more than the narrator says; end with a moment that reveals character.

items.stem: Which technique slows the pace at a climactic moment?
options: Summarising the action in one sentence
items.answer: Focusing on small sensory details
items.markingKey: Close detail stretches time and heightens tension.

items.stem: This extract uses foreshadowing: ‘If I had known then what the stranger wanted, I would never have opened the door.’ Explain how it builds suspense.
items.answer: Foreshadowing: a hint of danger to come.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying foreshadowing; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: a hint of danger to come.

items.stem: This extract uses short sentences and fragments: ‘He ran. Left. Right. A dead end.’ Explain how it builds suspense.
items.answer: Short sentences and fragments: the fragments speed up pace and mimic panic.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for identifying short sentences and fragments; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: the fragments speed up pace and mimic panic.

items.stem: Identify the technique, analyse its effect, and continue the extract for two or three sentences, maintaining the tension: ‘He ran. Left. Right. A dead end.’
items.answer: Short sentences and fragments: the fragments speed up pace and mimic panic. Continuation should sustain the technique.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for short sentences and fragments; 1 for effect; remaining mark(s) for a continuation that sustains tension.

items.stem: Identify the technique, analyse its effect, and continue the extract for two or three sentences, maintaining the tension: ‘A single bead of sweat ran down the guard’s neck and disappeared into his collar.’
items.answer: Focusing on small sensory details: close focus slows time and heightens tension. Continuation should sustain the technique.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for focusing on small sensory details; 1 for effect; remaining mark(s) for a continuation that sustains tension.

items.stem: Write a story called ‘Footsteps’ in which suspense builds to a dramatic climax. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: establish normality briefly; introduce a threat or deadline; tighten pace with shorter sentences; slow down at the climax with sensory detail; release tension in the resolution.

items.stem: When does a new line (paragraph) begin in written dialogue?
options: Only at the end of the conversation
Each time a different character speaks
items.answer: Each time a different character speaks
items.markingKey: New speaker, new line.

items.stem: ‘“Tired?” said Auntie Grace, handing me a suitcase’ (a narrative extract, ‘Auntie Grace Arrives’). What does the phrase ‘Tired?’ suggest, and how might it make the reader feel?
items.answer: echoing the mother’s word as a question shows Grace’s sharp, combative wit.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘Tired?’. Model point: echoing the mother’s word as a question shows Grace’s sharp, combative wit. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: In a narrative extract, ‘Auntie Grace Arrives’: ‘“Well,” she said. “I suppose it has character.”’ What does this line reveal about Auntie Grace?
items.answer: She is critical and snobbish, delivering an insult disguised as politeness.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: critical/snobbish; polite surface hides criticism

items.stem: Read ‘“Tired?” said Auntie Grace, handing me a suitcase’ from a narrative extract, ‘Auntie Grace Arrives’. Name the language feature, quote the key words and explain how they shape the reader’s response.
items.answer: Dialogue (‘Tired?’): echoing the mother’s word as a question shows Grace’s sharp, combative wit.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (dialogue); 1 for selecting the key words ‘Tired?’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. echoing the mother’s word as a question shows Grace’s sharp, combative wit.

items.stem: Identify the technique used in ‘“I am seventy-four, child. I have been tired since 1987.”’ (a narrative extract, ‘Auntie Grace Arrives’) and analyse its effect on the reader.
items.answer: Hyperbole (‘tired since 1987’): her dry, exaggerated reply is comic and shows her sharp wit and self-importance.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (hyperbole); 1 for selecting the key words ‘tired since 1987’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. her dry, exaggerated reply is comic and shows her sharp wit and self-importance.

items.stem: Write a story in which most of the tension comes from a conversation between a parent and teenager on a long car journey. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: establish setting briefly; let the conversation between a parent and teenager on a long car journey carry the conflict; use subtext, interruptions and silences; end on a line of dialogue or a telling action.

items.stem: What is an epiphany in a story?
options: A sudden moment of realisation or insight for a character
A twist caused by a stranger
items.answer: A sudden moment of realisation or insight for a character
items.markingKey: Often the turning point of a quiet ending.

items.stem: Why is ‘it was all a dream’ usually a weak ending?
options: It must be written in the past tense
It cancels the events and the reader’s investment
items.answer: It cancels the events and the reader’s investment
items.markingKey: Examiners see it as avoiding resolution.

items.stem: This is an example of epiphany: ‘Only then did I understand that my grandfather had never been lost at all; he had simply been going home.’ Explain why it might be an effective way to end a story.
items.answer: Epiphany: a sudden realisation reframes earlier events.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying epiphany; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: a sudden realisation reframes earlier events.

items.stem: Rewrite this weak ending so that it has more impact. ‘And then I woke up and it was all a dream.’
items.answer: Model: replace with a resolution that follows from the events, e.g. a final image that shows how the character has changed.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for an ending that avoids the weakness (cancels the story and cheats the reader’s investment), is earned by the story and leaves a strong final impression. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: A student has discovered that her best friend lied about a scholarship. Write the final section of this story (an epiphany), making sure the ending has impact. Write about 200–250 words.
items.answer: Model approach: bring the central conflict to a head; choose a an epiphany; end with an image or line that echoes the opening or theme.

items.stem: What is the climax of a narrative?
options: The point of highest tension where the central conflict comes to a head
items.answer: The point of highest tension where the central conflict comes to a head
items.markingKey: Everything builds to it; the resolution follows.

items.stem: This plan uses a frame narrative structure: ‘An old woman tells her granddaughter the story of her journey across the border; we return to them at the end.’ Explain how this structure could make the story more effective.
items.answer: Frame narrative: a story within a story, framed by the present-day conversation.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for identifying frame narrative; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: a story within a story, framed by the present-day conversation.

items.stem: Identify the structure in this plan and explain one advantage and one risk of using it in an exam composition: ‘Start with the narrator trapped in a lift, then fill in how they got there, then the rescue.’
items.answer: In medias res: the story opens at a dramatic moment and explains afterwards. Risk: confusing time shifts or running out of words before the resolution.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for in medias res; 1 for an advantage; 1 for a risk; further marks for developed explanation.

items.stem: Which type of narrative voice is used here? ‘I did not take the money. I merely borrowed it without asking, which is completely different.’
items.answer: unreliable narrator
items.markingKey: Unreliable narrator: the narrator’s self-justification shows their account cannot be trusted.

items.stem: This extract uses a naive narrator: ‘The man next door is a spy. I know because he has three bins and nobody needs three bins.’ Explain the effect of this voice on the reader.
items.answer: Naive narrator: the child’s comic logic reveals innocence.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for identifying naive narrator; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: the child’s comic logic reveals innocence.

items.stem: Identify the technique used in ‘If the house explodes, I would like it known that I was against the vacuum cleaner from the start.’ (a narrative extract, ‘My Brother the Genius’) and analyse its effect on the reader.
items.answer: Hyperbole (‘If the house explodes’): the exaggerated, formal disclaimer is comic and shows the narrator’s dry, teenage voice.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (hyperbole); 1 for selecting the key words ‘If the house explodes’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the exaggerated, formal disclaimer is comic and shows the narrator’s dry, teenage voice.

items.stem: This extract uses a ticking clock: ‘The countdown on the screen read 00:47. Then 00:46.’ Explain how it builds suspense.
items.answer: A ticking clock: the visible countdown increases pressure.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying a ticking clock; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: the visible countdown increases pressure.

items.stem: Identify the technique used in ‘Somewhere far above us, a cable groaned.’ (a narrative extract, ‘Floor Nineteen’) and analyse its effect on the reader.
items.answer: Personification (‘groaned’): the cable seems to be in pain, suggesting it may break and building dread.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (personification); 1 for selecting the key words ‘groaned’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the cable seems to be in pain, suggesting it may break and building dread.

items.stem: Read a narrative extract, ‘Floor Nineteen’. ‘The lift shuddered, dropped a few centimetres and stopped. For a moment nobody spoke. The light above the doors flickered between 18 and 19, as if it could not decide. Then it went out. In the darkness I heard the man beside me begin to breathe faster, short dry gasps, and the woman in the corner whispered something in a language I did not know. I pressed the alarm. Nothing. I pressed it again and held it until my thumb ached. Somewhere far above us, a cable groaned. Then, very softly, the floor began to tilt.’ How does the writer build tension in this extract? Support your answer with close reference to the text.
items.answer: In medias res; short sentences and fragments; sensory details in darkness; personified light and cable; repeated failed actions; slow, soft final cliffhanger.

Indicative content: In medias res; short sentences and fragments; sensory details in darkness; personified light and cable; repeated failed actions; slow, soft final cliffhanger.

items.stem: In a narrative extract, ‘Auntie Grace Arrives’ the writer uses the hyperbole ‘tired since 1987’: ‘“I am seventy-four, child. I have been tired since 1987.”’ Explain what it suggests to the reader.
items.answer: her dry, exaggerated reply is comic and shows her sharp wit and self-importance.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘tired since 1987’. Model point: her dry, exaggerated reply is comic and shows her sharp wit and self-importance. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Rewrite this reported speech as direct dialogue that reveals the characters’ feelings. Punctuate it correctly. ‘The coach told the team that they had played badly and that he was disappointed.’
items.answer: Model: The coach waited until the door closed. “That,” he said quietly, “was the worst half I have ever watched.”
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for correct punctuation and layout; dialogue revealing character/subtext; a supporting action or gesture. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.answer: Model approach: bring the central conflict to a head; choose a a circular ending; end with an image or line that echoes the opening or theme.

items.stem: Why should you plan the ending before you start writing?
options: So that you can build towards it and avoid a rushed or random conclusion
So you can write it first
Because the ending must be a twist
items.answer: So that you can build towards it and avoid a rushed or random conclusion
items.markingKey: Planning endings helps control structure (W2).

items.stem: This plan uses a frame narrative structure: ‘A diary found in an attic tells most of the story; the finder’s reaction closes it.’ Explain how this structure could make the story more effective.
items.answer: Frame narrative: the found diary is framed by the finder’s story.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for identifying frame narrative; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: the found diary is framed by the finder’s story.

items.stem: Plan a narrative composition called ‘The Last Train’ using an in medias res structure. Outline the opening, the rising action, the climax and the resolution in one or two lines each.
items.answer: Model: opening that hooks (consistent with a in medias res structure); rising complications; a single clear climax; a resolution that links back to the title ‘The Last Train’.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: structure clearly in medias res; focused plot; clear climax; resolution earned and linked to the title; realistic for 350–450 words.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is a naive narrator? (b) What makes a narrative voice ‘distinctive’?
items.answer: (a) A narrator who does not fully understand what they describe, while the reader does (b) A consistent, recognisable personality conveyed through vocabulary, rhythm and attitude
items.markingKey: (a) Often a child; creates dramatic irony. (b) E.g. the dry humour of a teenage narrator.

items.stem: Explain the effect of the words ‘revising the ceiling’ in this line from a narrative extract, ‘My Brother the Genius’: ‘So I am lying on the sofa, revising the ceiling.’
items.answer: the joke reveals the narrator is not revising at all, creating a comic, self-aware voice.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘revising the ceiling’; 1 for the effect on the reader, mood or idea created; 1 for a developed point that explores a second connotation or links to the wider text. Model point: the joke reveals the narrator is not revising at all, creating a comic, self-aware voice. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Situation: A family’s car breaks down on a desert road at night. Write the opening paragraph of this story using a retrospective adult narrator. Make the voice distinctive.
items.answer: Any opening with a sustained retrospective adult narrator: consistent perspective, characteristic vocabulary and attitude, and details that reveal character.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: voice clearly a retrospective adult narrator; sustained and distinctive; character revealed through detail; accurate expression.

items.stem: Explain the effect of the words ‘as if it could not decide’ in this line from a narrative extract, ‘Floor Nineteen’: ‘The light above the doors flickered between 18 and 19, as if it could not decide.’
items.answer: the hesitating light mirrors the uncertainty of the passengers and stretches the moment.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘as if it could not decide’. Model point: the hesitating light mirrors the uncertainty of the passengers and stretches the moment. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Rewrite this flat narrative so that it builds tension and suspense. ‘We were climbing the mountain and the weather got bad and we had to go down quickly.’
items.answer: Model: At noon the sky was blue. By one, a grey wall had swallowed the summit. The wind found every gap in my jacket, and when Kofi shouted, the words were torn away before they reached me.

items.stem: Write a story called ‘The Signal’ in which suspense builds to a dramatic climax. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: establish normality briefly; introduce a threat or deadline; tighten pace with shorter sentences; slow down at the climax with sensory detail; release tension in the resolution.

items.stem: ‘handing me a suitcase that weighed as much as I did’ (a narrative extract, ‘Auntie Grace Arrives’). What does the phrase ‘weighed as much as I did’ suggest, and how might it make the reader feel?
items.answer: the exaggeration adds humour and shows Grace treating the narrator as a porter.

items.stem: Explain why this ending is weak and how it could be improved: ‘Suddenly a helicopter appeared and rescued everyone. The end.’
items.answer: Weakness: a coincidence solves the problem (deus ex machina); no character agency. Model: let the character solve the problem through an earlier-planted skill or decision.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies weakness; suggests a valid improvement.

items.stem: Read the ending of a short story, ‘The Photograph’. ‘I found the photograph on the last day, when the house was empty and the removal van was already turning the corner. It had slipped behind the radiator: my father at twenty, younger than my brother is now, standing on a beach I had never seen, laughing at something outside the frame. All my life I had known him as a careful man, a man who checked the locks twice and never sang. I had not known he could laugh like that. I put the photograph in my pocket and stood for a long time in the bare kitchen. Then I locked the door – once – and walked down the hill towards the station, and I did not check it again.’ How does the writer create an effective ending to the story? Support your answer with close reference to the text.
items.answer: Setting of departure; discovery of the photograph; contrast between the father the narrator knew and the young man; quiet epiphany; circular echo of the locks; understated final sentence.
